title: Recomp guide (part.1): What it is & isn't
summary: First part of NH's recomp series. He defines a recomp as staying at the same bodyweight while gaining strength and muscle and losing fat, describes his own 7-8 month recomp at 210 lbs after a panic cut from 240, explains how to monitor it, and argues it is a slow, unsexy but often better alternative to bulk/cut cycles.

claims.claim: A recomp means staying at the same bodyweight while gaining strength, losing fat and gaining muscle.
The best time to start a recomp is when you're fluffier, usually after a bulk, not after a big cut.
He overbulked to 240 lbs, panic-cut about 30 lbs in a month to around 210, and lost mostly water and muscle rather than fat, so he stayed fairly high bodyfat.
After that he quit bulk/cut cycles because they were getting him nowhere, and started recomping at 210 lbs without any research.
The idea that only a caloric surplus or deficit exists is wrong; YouTube fitness pushes bulk/cut because the payoffs (abs, strength, measurements) come fast.
Natural bodybuilding is a game of patience; recomps are rarely discussed because they're slow, unsexy and hard to sell.
He has held the same bodyweight for 7 months, weighing himself only every month or two without obsessing.
During his recomp his squat, deadlift, lower-body lifts and curls went up, while bench and overhead press stagnated or regressed; fat cushioning helps presses more than other lifts.
Don't test bodyfat every two weeks. Monitor a recomp by weight every few months, strength or tonnage trending up, and how your body looks.
His reasoning: a body under heavy training volume at maintenance wants to make the work easier, so it trades fat for muscle.
Eating at maintenance while sedentary gives a reverse recomp: you lose muscle and gain fat because the body doesn't need the muscle.
Gaining weight is a slow bulk and losing weight is a slow cut; a recomp means staying at the same weight.
You can't recomp fast; the body takes time to learn to prioritize muscle and stop storing fat, just as you're weak at the start of a cut and don't gain bench instantly on a bulk.
A recomp should last at least a year; if you overbulked to 18-19% bodyfat, stay on it until around 12-13%.
His measurements are either rising or holding with none dropping, so he believes he is trading fat for muscle.
He thinks recomping is usually more beneficial than bulking and cutting, especially past a certain level.
